title: Rectifying market externalities via AI policymaking
abstract: Abstract Traditional competitive markets do not account for negative externalities; indirect costs that some participants impose on others, such as the cost of over-appropriating a common-pool resource (which diminishes future stock, and thus harvest, for everyone). Quantifying appropriate interventions to market prices has proven to be quite challenging. We propose a practical approach to computing market prices and allocations via a deep reinforcement learning policymaker agent, operating in an environment of other learning agents. Our policymaker allows us to tune the prices with regard to diverse objectives such as sustainability and resource wastefulness, fairness, buyers’ and sellers’ welfare, etc. As a highlight of our findings, our policymaker is significantly more successful in maintaining resource sustainability , compared to the market equilibrium outcome, in scarce resource environments.
venue: Autonomous Agents and Multi-Agent Systems

title: Did Nationwide Mental Health Insurance Reform in Israel Increase Access to Community-Based Care?
abstract: Abstract Israel’s nationwide mental health reform (July 1, 2015) transferred responsibility and funding for mental healthcare from the Ministry of Health to Israel’s four Health Maintenance Organizations (HMOs), aiming to improve access and availability, integrate mental health into general care, and shift delivery toward community-based models. Using electronic health records and administrative data from all four HMOs and the Ministry of Health, we assessed longitudinal trends in mental health service utilization from 2012 to 2019 among continuously insured Israeli residents with any recorded mental health diagnosis, mental health–related service contact, or psychotropic medication dispensing (31% of the national population). Outcomes included annual community-based mental health visits in HMO clinics, outpatient psychiatric visits in hospital clinics, mental health–related emergency department (ED) visits, psychiatric hospitalizations, and psychiatric medication dispensed. Post-reform changes were examined using Poisson regression adjusted for age, sex, social group, and socioeconomic status. Post-reform, community-based visits increased fourfold and hospital outpatient visits increased 3.3-fold. Psychiatric medication dispensing rose by 56% (psychostimulants + 87%; antidepressants + 60%). ED visits without admission increased by 40% while admission rates remained stable; total hospitalizations increased by 10%. Women had higher outpatient and medication use, whereas men had higher ED and inpatient use. Adjusted models indicated a 16% post-reform increase in service utilization ( P < .0001). During 2015–2019, we analyzed 265,286 mental health–related ED visits; 77% occurred in psychiatric-hospital EDs and 23% in general-hospital EDs, and most visits did not result in hospitalization (78% in general hospitals; 67% in psychiatric hospitals). Overall, Israel’s reform was associated with system-wide expansion and a shift toward community-based care, alongside rising non-admission ED presentations, warranting further research on pathways, clinical need, and follow-up, and on strengthening accessible community-based urgent and crisis alternatives to ED care.
venue: Administration and Policy in Mental Health and Mental Health Services Research

title: The Promise and Practice of Sharing Qualitative Data in Communication Research: Insights from the Qualitative Data Repository
abstract: As open science ideas gain traction in communication and media studies, qualitative researchers face unique challenges and opportunities in adopting transparent and reproducible practices. This article contributes to the growing conversation on open research infrastructures by introducing the Qualitative Data Repository (QDR) as a domain-specific solution for qualitative and multi-method data sharing. QDR is particularly well-equipped to manage data derived from human participants or existing media materials, both of which are widely used in this field. We explore how QDR’s infrastructure, services, and ethical frameworks can be adapted to the needs of communication scholars. First, we briefly outline the benefits of qualitative data sharing—including increased transparency, methodological rigor, and pedagogical value—while acknowledging possible barriers such as ethical concerns, time constraints, and disciplinary histories. We then review practical developments that have taken place over the last five years by scholars practicing some of the principles for trustworthy qualitative communication research laid out by Humphreys et al. (2021). Using examples from a wide variety of projects where QDR has already facilitated data publication and annotations for transparent inquiry, we illustrate how similar practices can be adopted systematically in communication research. We also highlight QDR’s support for researchers throughout the data lifecycle, from planning and consent to curation and controlled access. This article aims to demystify qualitative data sharing and encourage broader adoption among communication and media studies scholars by showcasing QDR’s model and its alignment with findable, accessible, interoperable, reusable principles. We argue that embracing more open and transparent research practices not only enhances the quality and visibility of individual projects but also fosters a more inclusive and collaborative scholarly community.
venue: Cogitatio (Cogitatio)

title: Get Back: The Delaware Supreme Court Discourages Appraisal Arbitrage in DFC Global Corporation v. Muirfield Value Partners, L.P.
abstract: This Casebrief examines the Delaware Supreme Court’s decision in DFC Global Corp. v. Muirfield Value Partners, L.P. and argues that the court appropriately curtailed appraisal arbitrage in clean mergers while preserving judicial discretion to protect minority shareholders in conflicted transactions. Rejecting a formal presumption that merger price equals fair value, the court nevertheless held that substantial weight should be given to the deal price when a company is sold through a robust, arm’s-length market process. The Casebrief contends that this approach aligns with recent legislative efforts to discourage appraisal arbitrage, reduces incentives for speculative appraisal litigation, and preserves appraisal rights where minority shareholder exploitation remains a concern.[This abstract was written by Microsoft Copilot, a generative artificial intelligence.]

title: Exploring Subjectivity Types of Community Health Visiting Nurses' Core Competencies: A Q-Methodological Approach
abstract: Purpose: This study aimed to identify subjective types of core competencies among community health visiting nurses.Methods: Q-methodology, which focuses on individual subjectivity, was applied. Thirty-two Q-statements were selected and ranked by 40 community health visiting nurses using a forced 9-point distribution from May 10 to June 30, 2025. The data were analyzed using the Personal Computer - Q methodology Analysis(PC-QUANL) program.Results: Four types were identified: the client-centered relational care type (Type I), collaborative decision-making and resource coordination type (Type II), clinical expertise and judgment type (Type III), and community resource linkage type (Type IV). The four types accounted for 52.9% of the total variance, with explanatory powers of 39.6% (Type I), 5.0% (Type II), 4.9% (Type III), and 3.4% (Type IV). Across the types, trust-based relationships emerged as a recurrent priority, whereas collaboration and resource coordination, clinical expertise and judgment, and community resource linkage differentiated the types.Conclusion: These findings clarify how community health visiting nurses subjectively prioritize core competencies and may be considered when designing competency education and ongoing competency-development strategies for these nurses.
venue: Research in Community and Public Health Nursing

title: The Role of Digital Wallets and UPI in Achieving Financial Empowerment for Underserved Populations in Emerging Markets
abstract: Abstract An analysis studies on the impact of digital wallets on India's financial inclusion and investigated the influence of the Unified Payment Interface (UPI) on resident’s banking activity. India's payments system processed more than 172 billion UPI transactions worth more than Rs. 260 lakh crore in FY25. This study explored the contribution of such a significant number of transactions to the financial empowerment of the population using UPI. This study utilised NPCI data, RBI reports, and field observations in Indian villages to understand the scale of the phenomenon and evaluate whether and how digital payments tools transform people's attitudes towards money. Analysis revealed that UPI usage in urban India exceeds 78%, while Indian rural women only use it at 28%. Thus, UPI usage is lower in India's rural areas than in urban regions, but it seems to be growing steadily. This article contains the statistics on adoption rates and seven barriers to entry, including policy recommendations on how to address them. It is observed that India's experience with financial technology is not inherently exclusionary, but careful consideration of several variables is needed to ensure that everyone can benefit from technology-enabled financial inclusion.
venue: Zenodo (CERN European Organization for Nuclear Research)

title: Experiencing AI Together: A Design-Based Research Approach to Collaborative Prompting in Education
abstract: Slides of the presentation at ICL2026 (TH Köln, Cologne, Germany). The talk reports on a Design-Based Research study on collaborative prompting in teacher education using the platform collab.prompting.school with in-house LLM hosting. Building on the RETURN Manifesto, it explores how AI use can become observable, discussable and revisable without requiring learners to disclose their full private AI histories. Baseline surveys show that about 70% of participants were reluctant to share their entire prompt history, while they engaged productively with controlled collaborative prompting across four settings. Qualitative feedback shows that prompt revision became central, suggesting that collaborative prompting should make revision pedagogically visible rather than focusing only on final artefacts or best prompts.
venue: TUGraz OPEN Library (Graz University of Technology)

title: Disciplined Integration: AI and the Legal Profession’s Existing Duties
abstract: Abstract This article argues that the legal profession’s existing duties of competence, supervision, candour, confidentiality, and procedural fairness provide the necessary framework for integrating generative AI into legal practice, without requiring a wholly new regulatory paradigm. Narrowing its focus to transformer-based large language models, the article examines the ‘fake law’ phenomenon, where models generate plausible but non-existent authorities, and traces its implications for miscarriages of justice, particularly where adversarial safeguards are thinnest: self-represented litigants, resource-constrained parties, and off-record settlements. It then considers AI in adjudication, arguing that transparency, contestability, and human-authored reasons remain non-negotiable for judicial legitimacy. The central recommendation is disciplined augmentation, not automation: AI should operate within the profession’s existing load-bearing beams through auditable workflows, clear disclosure norms, and continuous education. Used with discipline, AI can strengthen practice; used without it, it risks eroding the trust and outcomes the profession exists to protect.
venue: Bond Law Review

title: Mitigating Climate Change Risks by Adopting Emerging Technologies: A Contextual Comparative Exploration of Fast Fashion Supply Chains
abstract: Abstract Empirical research suggests that the fast fashion (FF) industry is a major contributor to global climate change. Fast-fashion supply chains (FFSCs) are inherently complex due to the multiplicity of processes, locations, and stakeholders involved. This research explores the key climate change risks, response strategies, and application of emerging technologies in the comparative context of developing and developed countries. Institutional theory was used as a theoretical lens, and the research data were collected by using expert interviews from industry experts in Pakistan and the UK. The analysis shows numerous climate change risks posed by FFSC at multiple tiers, ranging from raw materials to the retailing of products. The FF industry in Pakistan is more focused on meeting the needs of UK fashion brands by adopting global frameworks to reduce their greenhouse gas emissions, including using sustainable materials and adopting changes according to the environmental standards and renewable energy due to coercive, normative, and mimetic pressures. In contrast, coercive and mimetic pressures forcing UK fashion companies to address regulatory and economic challenges and deal with persistent organisational and cultural issues including fast-changing customer requirements. To mitigate climate change risks, companies in both contexts are adopting emerging technologies such as AI-based analytics, internet of things, automation, blockchain and digital traceability-based solutions, and 3D printing. However, they face challenges such as high initial costs, human capital gaps, and data integration issues. To mitigate these challenges, companies in both contexts are adopting strategies such as technology–business alignment, collaboration with technology partners and multiple stakeholders, pilot testing of new technologies, cultural transformation, and structural changes.
venue: Management International Review

title: Decoding technology transition process through consumer behavior: experience from China’s electric vehicle evolution
abstract: The competition between electric vehicles (EVs) and internal combustion engine vehicles is fundamentally shaped by how heterogeneous consumers respond to technological and market change. This study develops a decision-based framework that links micro-level adoption behavior with macro-level fleet dynamics. Using China as the core case, we identify three consumer segments: new, replacement, and renewal buyers, and show that they react differently to purchase cost, usability, and charging conditions. Embedding these segments in a dynamic simulation suggests a conditional phased transition under the baseline scenario: EV stock may overtake ICEVs around 2030, and the expansion of the secondhand EV market after 2035 could reshape buyer composition and strengthen the role of replacement demand. A cross-national comparison of 51 countries further shows that economic development stages and institutional capacity mediate how these behavioral logics translate into market outcomes, from infrastructure and affordability constraints in emerging EV markets to norm-driven, autonomous adoption in advanced EV markets. The findings highlight that EV transitions are driven by the interaction between consumer heterogeneity and market development, providing a behavioral basis for stage-specific policies and infrastructure strategies worldwide.
venue: Humanities and Social Sciences Communications

title: Does sleep matter for recovery after stroke? Functional severity shapes the association between sleep and functional outcome during inpatient stroke rehabilitation
abstract: Abstract Background Sleep disturbances are common after stroke and have been associated with rehabilitation outcomes. The clinical meaning of post-stroke sleep duration remains unclear, as longer sleep may be associated with different clinical and functional states, including greater disability. This exploratory study investigated the relationship between sleep and functional outcome during stroke rehabilitation, and the moderating role of baseline functional status. Methods Twenty-nine patients with stroke underwent a 10-day longitudinal monitoring protocol during rehabilitation. Functional independence and motor performance were assessed at the beginning (T0) and the end (T1) of the observation period using the Barthel Index, 10-Meter Walk Test, and 9-Hole Peg Test. Sleep was assessed throughout the monitoring period using sleep diaries, and actigraphy . Results Functional independence improved from T0 to T1, whereas motor performance did not significantly change. In unadjusted analyses, longer actigraphy-derived total sleep time and longer self-reported total time in bed were correlated with lower Barthel Index scores at T1. Moderation analyses adjusted for prior rehabilitation days showed that longer total sleep time was positively associated with Barthel Index at T1 only in patients with higher baseline independence, while longer time in bed was positively associated at average and higher baseline levels. Conclusions The associations between sleep duration or time in bed and later post-rehabilitation functional independence vary according to baseline functional status. Given the small sample size and observational design, these findings should be interpreted cautiously and considered preliminary and hypothesis-generating.
venue: Neurological Sciences

title: President’s Column: Make the Most of ATCE 2026: A Strategic Investment in Your Career and Organization
abstract: _ October is an exciting time for SPE members around the world because it means the Annual Technical Conference and Exhibition (ATCE) is nearly here. This year, ATCE will take place 21–23 October, at the George R. Brown Convention Center in Houston. Whether you are an experienced technical professional, an emerging leader, a student, a young professional, an executive, an entrepreneur, or a job seeker, ATCE offers opportunities to learn, build relationships, and advance your career. The key is to approach the conference with a plan and a clear understanding of the value you want to gain, as well as the value you can bring back to your organization. A Strategic Investment in Knowledge and Capability ATCE brings together technical experts, industry leaders, innovators, service providers, and energy professionals from around the world. The program provides access to the latest technical information, case studies, emerging technologies, best practices, and practical solutions addressing some of the industry’s most important challenges. For many attendees, the greatest value begins with the technical program. Before arriving, take time to review the agenda and identify the technical sessions, special sessions, strategic panels, and general sessions most relevant to your responsibilities and professional interests. Consider attending ticketed events such as Technical Section Receptions, the Keynote Luncheon, the Awards Banquet, and the President’s Luncheon and Annual Meeting of Members. Divide coverage of important sessions so that your organization can maximize its investment and benefit from a broader range of presentations and discussions. After the conference, share key insights, lessons learned, new technologies, and industry contacts with your colleagues. This approach transforms ATCE from an individual professional development activity into an investment that benefits the entire organization. A strong business case should clearly connect the ATCE program with your role, responsibilities, and your organization’s objectives. For a sample justification letter, find it here on the ATCE registration page under FAQs and Justification Letter. ATCE offers a unique opportunity to gain actionable knowledge from experts and leaders across the energy industry. The program includes conceptual technologies, case studies, lessons learned, and practical solutions that can help professionals address technical and business challenges more effectively.

title: Green consumer behavior in e-commerce: The mediating role of digital engagement and the moderating effects of literacy and environmental knowledge
abstract: This study aims to identify the factors influencing digital engagement behavior and online shopping intention in the context of green e-commerce. Extending prior studies that have often examined green consumption, mobile shopping experience, and platform sustainability as separate research streams, this study develops an integrated model explaining how value-related, brand-related, experience-related, and platform-related factors jointly shape green e-commerce behavior through digital engagement. Data were collected from consumers in Vietnam through a quantitative survey and analyzed using partial least squares structural equation modeling (PLS-SEM). The results show that green perceived value, eco-brand credibility, mobile shopping experience, and platform sustainability features positively influence digital engagement behavior and online shopping intention. Furthermore, digital engagement behavior plays an important mediating role, clarifying the behavioral mechanism through which consumers move from green awareness and digital platform experience to online shopping intention. Meanwhile, digital literacy and environmental knowledge significantly strengthen the effect of digital engagement behavior on online shopping intention, demonstrating the important role of these competencies in sustainable consumption. By integrating green value perception, eco-brand credibility, mobile shopping experience, platform sustainability features, digital engagement, and consumer competencies into a single explanatory framework, this study offers novel evidence on green e-commerce behavior in an emerging economy context. This study contributes to expanding the understanding of green consumer behavior on digital platforms and proposes strategic directions for e-commerce businesses seeking to promote sustainable online consumption.
venue: Heliyon

title: Effect on Decision Making Processes of Pythagorean Fuzzy Set
abstract: Pythagorean Fuzzy Set concept is a more flexible approach that encompasses fuzzy sets and intuitionistic fuzzy sets in the uncertainty modeling process. The concept offers a new approach for jointly evaluating membership and non-membership degrees. This approach allows decision makers to express uncertainty over a wider range. Therefore, Pythagorean fuzzy sets offer higher representational power than intuitionistic fuzzy sets and are particularly effective in solving complex problems such as multi-criteria decision making, risk analysis, expert systems. Decision making is an approach that aims to systematically analyze decision problems that consider multiple criteria. This method allows the decision maker to evaluate both qualitative and quantitative factors to make the most appropriate choice among alternatives. Among the most commonly used methods, AHP, TOPSIS and PROMETHEE are prominent, aiming to determine the relative advantages of alternatives under different assumptions. Today, fuzzy logic and its extended forms, intuitionistic and pythagorean fuzzy approaches, are frequently integrated into decision making processes to reduce the influence of uncertainty, expert judgment, and subjective assessments. This allows decision models to more effectively represent the complex and uncertain situations encountered in real life problems. This study presents an example of the impact of pythagorean fuzzy sets on decision-making processes.
venue: Turkish Journal of Science and Technology

title: From “curse” to “gospel”: how can industrial relocation lead cities to cross the resource dependence gap
abstract: Industrial relocation offers a novel solution to help mitigate the “resource curse” by reducing dependence on natural resources and fostering diversified economic systems, thereby optimizing the industrial structure. This paper explores the mechanism and economic consequences of industrial relocation’s dependence on the host country’s resources, focusing on the National Industrial Relocation Demonstration Zones (NIRDZ). Theoretical analysis using urban panel statistics from 2006 to 2022 investigates the relationship between industrial relocation and the host’s resource dependence through a multi-period Difference-in-Differences. The heterogeneity of the policy effect is analyzed from a three-dimensional urban attribute perspective encompassing “location-feature-scale.” The results indicate that: (1) Industrial relocation can significantly restrain resource dependence and thereby help alleviate the “resource curse,” a conclusion that remains valid following multiple robustness tests. (2) Industrial relocation mainly inhibits urban resource dependence by reducing energy consumption, increasing the level of foreign investment, and enhancing technological innovation. (3) Heterogeneity analysis demonstrates that the NIRDZ policy exerts a more pronounced inhibitory effect on resource dependence in central cities, non-provincial-capital cities, and cities with smaller populations. Unlike the cracking strategy proposed by most previous studies on resource management, this paper reveals that central cities can provide a viable pathway to alleviating the “resource curse” by developing industries in the eastern region. This not only establishes a foundation for decision-making regarding the green transformation and sustainable development of resource-rich cities but also contributes to new empirical evidence to the “resource curse” governance literature.
venue: Humanities and Social Sciences Communications

title: Framework for user-centred design and pre-occupancy design evaluation of higher education buildings
abstract: Purpose Higher education (HE) buildings often exhibit persistent performance gaps that compromise user comfort, health and satisfaction. These adverse outcomes are frequently linked to inadequate end-user engagement in the design phase. This study develops and validates a holistic framework for end-user engagement that systematically integrates user inputs throughout the design process to enable user-centred design and pre-occupancy evaluation, proactively mitigating performance gaps. Design/methodology/approach The framework was formulated through an integrative review and idea mapping from three knowledge areas: user engagement theories, functional performance specification and design elements. The framework was validated through 70 structured interviews: 35 with end-users, 17 with HE building professionals, and 18 with industry architects. Quantitative data were analysed using descriptive statistics, Kruskal–Wallis and Dunn tests. Qualitative insights were examined through content analysis. Findings The study presents a novel framework featuring a process-flow model and modules for user-requirements acquisition and design evaluation to engage end-users throughout HE building design. The framework’s overall effectiveness for end-user involvement across pre-design, schematic and detailed design was rated 8.4 out of 10. Study participants identified many benefits of the framework, including comprehensiveness, facilitation of end-user engagement across all design stages, adaptability, quantifiable scoring, stimulation of user reflection, ease of distribution and robustness. Originality/value The systemised framework addresses longstanding barriers to end-user engagement in HE building design. Its modular and traceable structure enables those with limited experience to implement structured engagement practices. By facilitating early, evidence-based user input, the framework promotes people-centred design, minimises post-occupancy modifications and enhances building performance and user satisfaction.

title: A Study on Educational Effects of Learner-Centered Generative AI-based Engineering Education Using AI Principle Cards
abstract: 최근 전 세계적으로 인공지능(AI: artificial intelligence) 전문 인력에 대한 수요가 급격히 증가하였으나, 국내 교육 체계의 한계로 인해 AI 인력 양성에 어려움을 겪고 있다. 이에 본 연구에서는 AI 교육지원 도구인 인공지능 원리카드(AIPC: AI principle card)를 개발하고, AIPC 기반의 교육 방법론을 구축하였다. AIPC는 예측형 및 생성형 AI의 개념, 원리, 활용 사례, 장단점 등을 시각화하였으며, 제안된 교육 방법론은 AIPC를 학습 과정에 통합한 학습 프로젝트로 설계되었다. 이를 학부생들에게 적용한 결과, 학습자들은 AI의 개념과 원리에 대한 이해도와 AI를 활용한 문제 해결 능력이 향상되었으며, AIPC와 교육 방법론에 대해 긍정적인 반응을 보였다.

title: How "Buy Now, Pay Later" Changes the Psychology of Spending" A Conceptual/Comparative Analysis of BNPL and the Traditional Credit Card
abstract: Abstract Buy now, pay later (BNPL) is typically described as either a harmless budgeting tool or a repackaged form of consumer debt. Neither framing explains why a product that charges no interest and divides a purchase into four small instalments has produced spending increases, delinquency patterns, nor was self-reported regret that closely resemble the credit card habits it intended to replace. This paper argues that BNPL and credit cards likely do not operate through the same psychological mechanism at different intensities, but through structurally different mechanisms that converge on similar financial harm. Drawing on Federal Reserve, CFPB, Central Bank of Ireland, and peer-reviewed data, the paper develops two original analytical tools: a taxonomy that separates six frequently conflated “BNPL effect” statistics according to what each actually measures and the strength of evidence behind it, and a framework termed the Debt Visibility Paradox, which decomposes “invisible debt” into four separately testable constructs — borrower recall, credit-bureau visibility, statement visibility, and cash-flow burden — rather than treating it as a single impression. The working conclusion is that BNPL may not so much reduce the pain of paying as redistribute it into units too small for existing disclosure rules to register.
venue: Zenodo (CERN European Organization for Nuclear Research)

title: Institute-created electronic flashcards, associated development effort, and exam performance in pharmacology education in human medicine
abstract: Abstract Electronic flashcards are popular among medical students, although their real-world effectiveness, and staff resources required to develop tailored decks, is not well understood. The Institute of Experimental and Clinical Pharmacology, Toxicology and Pharmacology of Natural Products at the Ulm University Medical Center, Germany, created 1007 flashcards on 228 drugs aligned to the local and national curriculum using the Anki flashcard software. The time needed for card development was documented. Medical students participated in an observational study over four semesters and were encouraged to use the cards alongside established study materials for exam preparation in clinical pharmacology. Exams concluded either a lecture-based course focusing on declarative knowledge, or concluded a seminar-based course focusing on case-based application. A survey assessed usage patterns and helpfulness of flashcards and other study materials, demographics, and self-rated general academic performance. Pseudonymous codes linked survey responses to individual exam scores. Flashcard use was reported by 38.4% of participants overall, with higher use when preparing for lecture-based exams than for seminar-based exams. In total, 83.3% of users considered the cards helpful. Participants with lower self-rated general academic performance were more likely to use flashcards. Flashcard users scored lower in the exam than non-users, but this association was no longer significant after adjusting for self-rated general academic performance. Flashcard development took on average 7 min per card. These findings suggest that academically weaker students, and students preparing for exams testing declarative knowledge, may prefer flashcards. Given the substantial staff time required, and the lacking benefit of our flashcard-decks, the decision to tailor curriculum-aligned flashcards should be made cautiously.
venue: Naunyn-Schmiedeberg s Archives of Pharmacology

title: Hitting Rewind: The Supreme Court of Pennsylvania in Trust Under Agreement of Taylor Signals a Move Away from Modern Developments of Trust Law by Requiring More Stringent Standards for Corporate Trustee Removal
abstract: This Casebrief examines the Supreme Court of Pennsylvania’s decision in Trust Under Agreement of Taylor and argues that the court narrowly limited beneficiaries’ ability to remove corporate trustees by holding that trustee removal must proceed exclusively under Section 7766 of the Uniform Trust Act. The Casebrief contends that the decision reinforces traditional deference to settlor intent while highlighting continuing concerns about the power imbalance between corporate trustees and beneficiaries.[This abstract was written by Microsoft Copilot, a generative artificial intelligence.]

title: From Innovation to Enterprise: the Role of Patent Law in Promoting Entrepreneurship and Start-Ups in India
abstract: AbstractInnovation drives entrepreneurship, technological progress and economic growth. For technology-based start-ups, patent protection helps transform innovative ideas into viable businesses by safeguarding inventions and facilitating investment, licensing, technology transfer and market expansion. This paper examines how patent law supports entrepreneurship and start-ups in India, focusing on the Patents Act, 1970, National IPR Policy, 2016, Start-up India and SIPP. It highlights challenges such as costs, limited awareness, procedural complexities and commercialization gaps. The study concludes that patents can promote innovation and competitiveness, but their success depends on broader support through finance, incubation, technology transfer and effective enforcement.
venue: Zenodo (CERN European Organization for Nuclear Research)

title: Customer Satisfaction In Public Sector Banks: Balancing The Digital Push And The Human Touch In India
abstract: Abstract The Indian banking sector has shifted dramatically from manual ledgers to advanced digital platforms. Public Sector Banks (PSBs), the backbone of the country’s financial system, have led this charge. Yet, despite heavy tech investments, customer satisfaction remains a pressing concern. This study explores the link between service quality, digital banking experience, and customer satisfaction in PSBs. Using a mixed-methods approach, we gathered data from 428 customers across urban and semi-urban areas in Karnataka, Maharashtra, and Tamil Nadu. Blending the SERVQUAL model with digital experience parameters, the findings show that while digital infrastructure has improved, the human element still dictates overall satisfaction. Customers like digital convenience but feel frustrated by poor grievance redressal and the digital divide affecting senior citizens. The study suggests a balanced "phygital" approach—using technology for efficiency while preserving the personal trust that remains a PSB's core strength.
venue: Zenodo (CERN European Organization for Nuclear Research)

title: A Wrinkle in Title VII: Rigid Evidentiary Requirements and Inadequate Causation Tests Trammel Women's Sex-Plus-Age Claims
abstract: This Comment examines the Tenth Circuit’s decision in Frappied v. Affinity Gaming Black Hawk, LLC and argues that, although the court recognized sex-plus-age claims under Title VII, older women remain disadvantaged by rigid comparator requirements and causation standards. The Comment contends that these doctrines make it difficult for women to prove discrimination based on the intersection of sex and age, particularly in appearance-driven industries where older male comparators are often unavailable. It concludes that the current framework limits the practical value of sex-plus-age claims and leaves many older women without an effective remedy for workplace discrimination.[This abstract was written by Microsoft Copilot, a generative artificial intelligence.]

title: A Comparative Study on Consumer Preferences and Buying Patterns between Organized and Unorganized Retail Formats in Maharashtra
abstract: Abstract Indian economy has grown rapidly in the last two decades, as a result of change in the business environment and thereby attracted massive investment from domestic and foreign players. This study is an effort to understand the revolution which has taken place in the Indian retail industry. Moreover, with the help of this study the researcher has made an attempt to analyze the shopping behaviour of consumer and try to assess consumer's perception with respect to organized retailer. In order to analyze the consumer's perception a survey has been conducted in Mumbai city and suburbs and based on the survey findings has been drawn by the researcher. The findings are based on the structured questionnaire collected from 100 respondents and the data has been collected through convenience sampling method. Organized retailer's popularity among the consumers is growing and thereby favouring the Mall culture which is quite prevalent in the Western Countries. Specially, youth prefer to shop more at modern retail formats as compared to consumer of adult and mature age groups. Moreover the research also highlight that Indian consumers are price sensitive also.

title: Beyond Magic and Godlike Authority Clarke's Third Law, Shermer's Last Law, and the Epistemology of AGI and SGI
abstract: Clarke’s Third Law and Shermer’s Last Law motivate a distinction between extraordinarycapability, accessible evidence, and attributed authority. We develop this distinction for artificialgeneral intelligence and superhuman general intelligence, including the conditional possibilitythat an AI invents useful mathematical metalanguages and teaches human-accessible fragments.Resource-bounded experiments, selected-demonstration models, checked proof transport, and ataught-observer theorem connect semantic learning to scoped decision risk. Public 2026 incidentdisclosures motivate a further distinction: understanding and final approval do not control effectsalready produced during loading, translation, evidence acquisition, memory consolidation,or tool use. Version 5 extends the outcome space from final answers to complete protected-effecttraces and explicitly models model identity, persistent memory, translation state, authorizationstate, and independently captured telemetry. New post-September-22 evidence includes aprovider-confirmed DNS path around an offline sandbox, provider-disclosed publication ofa secret token despite repeated human instructions, a demonstrated self-replicating promptinjectionmechanism confined to simulated tool calls, experimental evidence that local agents candelete their own traces, and new authorization research on provenance-bound memory, counterfactualpermission evaluation, and policy-constrained runtime validation. An integrity–behaviordecomposition and a history-uniform first-failure theorem separate behavioral reliability fromthe validity of enforcement and evidence boundaries. We add a trace-integrity bound, aversion-bound authorization model, and a state-transition rule that invalidates certificates afterunapproved model or interpreter mutation. Effect-preserving translation, policy automata,robust finite-state risk certificates, and pessimistic validation of incomplete traces provideexplicit proof obligations and counterexamples. Independent capability grants, out-of-bandenforcement, version-bound certificates, restricted teaching environments, and operationallyverified termination define a proposed architecture, not a claimed deployment achievement.Incident statements retain attribution and correction status; numerical fixtures are constructed,not empirical estimates. The contribution is a falsifiable account of expanding what humanscan verify without silently expanding what AI may do, not a universal safety guarantee orevidence of a superior AI metalanguage.
venue: Zenodo (CERN European Organization for Nuclear Research)

title: Local geographies of housing inequality: Neighbourhood trajectories of housing purchasing (un)affordability across neighbourhoods in England and Wales (2010-2023)
abstract: In recent decades, housing purchasing prices have outpaced incomes, increasing spatial inequalities and creating a growing challenge to homeownership. Despite housing markets being highly localised with most residential moves made at local scales, analyses of housing affordability have typically focused on national- and regional-level trends. We draw on a novel housing price dataset, to present the first neighbourhood-level analysis of housing (un)affordability trajectories across England and Wales (2010 to 2023). In doing so, we interrogate the reproduction of socio-spatial inequalities at the scale of everyday lives and raise questions about local geographies of housing inequality. We develop and map eight distinct neighbourhood trajectories of housing (un)affordability and reveal a nuanced geographical mosaic of housing (un)affordability across local areas. We show how different trajectories sit side-by-side, with localities of affordability in areas considered extremely unaffordable in aggregated analyses, such as London, and vice versa. While affordability pressures are experienced heterogeneously across the period, most neighbourhoods display a decline in affordability due to rising housing prices relative to incomes. Mapping these trajectories reveals a prominent spatial gradient in affordability pressures, which may narrow the ability of some residents to adjust to housing becoming less affordable, as surrounding areas are even less affordable. Overall, this geographically nuanced work illustrates unjust urban restructuring resulting from localised spatial manifestations of the financialisation of housing.
venue: Geoforum

title: On emotions and cooperative behavior for wildlife conservation
abstract: Abstract Emotions shape how people relate to wildlife, yet their role in encouraging cooperation for conservation has been largely overlooked in behavioral research. This study explores how emotional responses influence group decisions to support wildlife protection using an online experiment inspired by public goods games, an economic game often used to study cooperation in behavioral economics. A total of 246 participants, recruited via Amazon Mechanical Turk, were exposed to short video clips designed to trigger either positive or negative emotions. They were then asked to decide how much money to contribute to efforts aimed at conserving one of two species: the grey wolf ( Canis lupus ) or the wolverine ( Gulo gulo ). The results showed that emotions can influence willingness to cooperate, but their effects varied by species. Positive emotional states led to increased support for wolf conservation, while no clear effect was observed for the wolverine. Interestingly, when the same emotion was induced, financial contributions did not differ significantly between the two species. These findings suggest that emotional engagement, through positive messaging, may serve as an effective mechanism to promote cooperative behavior in wildlife conservation initiatives. However, the species-specific differences also highlight the importance of tailoring outreach and policy strategies to the emotional and cultural context surrounding each animal.
venue: European Journal of Wildlife Research

title: Multi-layer network analysis of deliberation in an online discussion platform: The case of Reddit
abstract: This paper proposes a novel multi-layer network model to study deliberation in online discussion platforms. The model comprises two layers: a discussion layer, which represents as a hierarchical tree the comment-to-comment replies within a given post, and an actor layer, which represents the actor-to-actor reply interactions. The interlayer links represent user-comment ownership. We use this network model to extend González-Bailón et al. (2010)’s foundational network analysis of argumentation and representation in discussion, by proposing two network metrics to measure the potential for deliberation in discussion threads. We also propose a new approach for identifying the boundaries that determine whether a given post is identified as deliberative, and for comparing the level of deliberation of collections of posts. We apply our new approach to a large Reddit dataset containing posts from 72 subreddits focused on different topics and demonstrate that our new metrics have construct validity in that observed differences in measured deliberation across categories of subreddits can be explained by the topics and purpose of the subreddits. While we find that some political subreddits exhibit high levels of deliberation thus indicating that online political talk can meet the prerequisites for deliberation, the level of deliberation in regional and sports subreddits was even higher. Analysis of the actor layer shows correlations between the deliberation measured on the discussion layer, and classical network metrics of the actor layer including degree distribution, assortativity, and the global clustering coefficient. These correlations reveal important insights into how the aggregate behaviour of users is related to deliberation.
venue: Social Networks

title: The Circular Loop Revisited: Vendor Financing in the Telecom Bubble and the AI Infrastructure Buildout
abstract: Abstract This study asks whether AI infrastructure financing in 2023-2026 shows warning signs like telecom vendor financing before the 2001 collapse. It uses a qualitative case study to compare selected telecom and AI financing ties across six measures: financing size, accounting treatment, loan terms, credit risk, the gap between infrastructure and revenue, and market stress. The results partly support the telecom-AI comparison, especially in the size of commitments and the growing infrastructure-to-revenue gap. Still, the financing structures change, the opposing parties are stronger, and widespread defaults have not appeared. The telecom experience is best used as an early-warning framework, not as proof that an AI collapse must follow.
venue: Zenodo (CERN European Organization for Nuclear Research)

title: Out of breath, out of mind: Competing frames and public support for carbon taxation in Spain
abstract: Efforts to implement climate policies often face public resistance. This study, based on a pre-registered survey experiment in Spain, tests how different framings of carbon taxation, emphasizing costs, primary climate benefits, co-benefits, and their combinations, shape public support. Compared to a baseline with no additional information, cost-focused messages reduce support, while benefit frames increase it; co-benefits (cleaner air, better health) produce the largest increase, though in isolation this is not statistically distinguishable from the primary-benefit frame. When paired with cost information, co-benefit framing sustains support more effectively than primary climate benefits, suggesting that immediate, tangible outcomes resonate more strongly with the public than distant climate goals. A dictionary-based analysis of open-ended responses corroborates this interpretation: co-benefit and cost treatments activate frame-aligned language, whereas the primary benefits treatment does not. The study further reveals systematic heterogeneity in responses: cost information reduces support most among left-leaning and lower-income respondents, while co-benefit framing is more persuasive among center- and right-leaning and higher-income respondents. Together, these findings point to a modest but systematic role of framing in shaping attitudes toward carbon taxation, with implications for designing more publicly acceptable climate policies.
venue: Electoral Studies

title: A partially time-changed Aït-Sahalia model: well-posedness and moment bounds
abstract: A partially time-changed Aït-Sahalia model is proposed, where the driving noise is a sub-diffusion process, also known as a time-changed Brownian motion. We prove that the model admits a unique global positive solution and establish positive and negative moment bounds. Finally, a truncated Euler–Maruyama discretization is used to provide numerical illustrations of sample paths and empirical moments.
venue: Fluctuation and Noise Letters

title: Towards On-Device Evidence Gathering for Intimate Partner Infiltration: A Feasibility Study for Joint Identity-Action Detection
abstract: Intimate Partner Infiltration (IPI) refers to phone-side privacy infiltration in intimate or close relationships, often enabled by physical access to a person's smartphone and discussed in technology-facilitated Intimate Partner Violence (IPV) contexts. Unlike conventional cyberattackers, IPI perpetrators leverage proximity and personal knowledge to circumvent standard protection, underscoring the need for targeted interventions, motivating device-side tools that surface such risk evidence for later review. While prior works have extensively studied IPV, and some have provided tailored and effective solutions such as security clinics, they are necessarily episodic and human-expert-intensive, and offer limited automated visibility into what happens on a smartphone between support sessions. Guided by a formative interview with experts (n=5), we take the first exploration into gathering IPI-risk evidence from a mobile system perspective and present AID, A utomated I PI D etection, a data-driven system that continuously logs unauthorized access and suspicious behaviors on smartphones. In a controlled 27-participant study, AID achieves an end-to-end F1 score of 0.928 with a 7.0% false positive rate for Top-1 phone-side risk flagging; when preserving top-3 candidate action categories as report context, AID achieves an F1 score of 0.981 and a false positive rate of 1.6%. These findings demonstrate AID's potential as an evidence-support tool that complements current clinic-based interpretation and safety-planning.
venue: Proceedings of the ACM on Interactive Mobile Wearable and Ubiquitous Technologies

title: How Much Do Airlines Make per Flight? Revenue and Net Profit per Departure of US Airlines from BTS Financial and T-100 Data, Company Annual Reports and IATA Industry Estimates, 2014–2026
abstract: Airlines do not publish revenue or profit per flight. We at Travel Statistics Bureau construct both for US domestic flying by dividing the domestic operating revenue and after-tax net income that US scheduled passenger airlines report to the Bureau of Transportation Statistics (BTS) by the domestic departures of the same airlines, matched carrier by carrier in the BTS T-100 segment data. In 2025 these airlines took in 187.8 billion across 7,838,856 domestic departures, or 23,958 per flight, and kept 3.2 billion, or about 408 per flight (402–415 given the rounding of the published total), 1.7% of revenue. Profit per flight was 71% below the 1,418 of 2019 and far below the 2015 peak of 2,506; in 2020 the average domestic flight lost 5,937. Revenue per flight, by contrast, has stayed above 23,000 since 2022. Industry operating revenue rose 28.7% between 2019 and 2025 while labour cost reached 91.2 billion, 37.8% of operating expenses and 1.84 times its 2016 level. Company annual reports give comparable figures for three groups that count their own flights: Southwest earned 311 per trip in 2025 against 1,682 in 2019, Alaska’s group 184 per departure, and Allegiant’s parent company lost 326 per departure, largely through resort charges. Dividing the International Air Transport Association’s worldwide net profit by its flight count gives about 1,157 per flight in 2025 and 594 in the 2026 forecast, when Middle East airlines are expected to move from 31.50 of profit per passenger to a loss of 21.40. All inputs are public.

title: Self-compassion is linked to positive affect and buffers declines in self-esteem
abstract: Abstract Successes and failures shape affective experiences and self-esteem. Self-compassion has been proposed as a protective factor, allowing individuals to acknowledge both strengths and shortcomings without excessive self-criticism. However, the mechanisms through which self-compassion influences changes in affect and self-esteem remain poorly understood. Here, we experimentally tested whether self-compassion modulates the links between performance feedback, affective experience and performance self-esteem. Participants completed an effortful performance task and received trial-by-trial feedback while repeatedly rating their positive affect, and reported on their state self-esteem both before and after the task. Results showed that self-compassion buffered against declines in performance self-esteem among poorly performing individuals, predicted higher overall positive affect throughout the task, and was associated with increased post-task performance self-esteem. Moreover, performance feedback predicted positive affect, and positive affect predicted post-task performance self-esteem, although these pathways were not moderated by self-compassion. Together, these findings add to the growing evidence of how self-compassion impacts positive affect and performance self-esteem, and may inform treatment strategies for clinical populations characterized by low self-esteem or heightened self-criticism.
venue: Royal Society Open Science

title: Two Modes of Reflection: How Temporal, Spatial, and Social Distances Affect Reflective Writing in Family Caregiving
abstract: Therapeutic writing offers significant benefits for well-being; however, for family caregivers, conventional fixed or user-initiated schedules often fail to align with their dynamic, high-stress reality. We conducted a three-week field study with 47 caregivers using a chatbot that delivered daily reflective writing cues and captured temporal, spatial, and social contexts. Our analysis identified a writing spectrum anchored by two distinct reflective modes. Under psychologically proximal conditions, participants produced detailed, emotion-rich, and care-recipient-focused narratives that supported emotional release. Under distal conditions, they generated calmer, self-focused, and analytic accounts that enabled objective reflection and cognitive reappraisal. Participants described trade-offs: proximity preserved vivid detail but limited objectivity, while distance enabled analysis but risked memory loss. This work contributes empirical evidence of how psychological distances shape reflective writing and proposes design implications for distance-aware Just-in-Time Adaptive Interventions for family caregivers' mental health support.
venue: Proceedings of the ACM on Interactive Mobile Wearable and Ubiquitous Technologies

title: Ease of Doing Business Reforms in India: A Legal and Public Analysis
abstract: Abstract The ease with which firms can establish themselves, operate, scale, and exit a market is closely linked to the quality of its legal and administrative institutions. Ease of Doing Business (EDB) has become a focal point of India’s economic policy in recent years. The reform agenda has moved beyond the removal of licensing hurdles and now includes digitalization, regulatory simplification, compliance reduction, insolvency reforms, taxation, single-window governance, and the rationalization of petty offenses. This paper attempts to assess India’s EDB reforms through the lens of legal and policy analysis. Reforming procedural bureaucracy is not the end goal – the emphasis is on whether legal and administrative changes have led to a significant improvement in terms of accessibility, predictability, efficiency, and cost reduction. The study tries to understand the constitutional underpinnings of economic freedoms, examines the laws and policies relating to corporate regulations, insolvency, taxation, digitalization, competitive federalism, and compliance reduction. It also analyses the reforms such as National Single Window System in terms of institutional mechanisms. The paper employs a doctrinal and qualitative research design. It focuses on the law, policy, and institutional mechanisms rather than quantifying the reform impact. Legal texts, policy documents, and scholarly literature are analysed to identify connections between procedural reforms and actual governance outcomes. The paper finds that India has made significant strides in reforming its regulatory framework but faces challenges in harmonizing diverse jurisdictions, reducing overlapping oversight, and removing protracted litigation. Digitalization reduces transaction costs, insolvency laws facilitate faster resolution of business closures, and compliance reduction initiatives target regulatory hurdles. However, inconsistent implementation, judicial delays, regulatory complexities, and disproportionate cost-benefit for small-scale enterprises remain pertinent issues. The paper concludes that India needs to shift from the EDB paradigm and focus on Ease of Complying, Competing, and Resolving Disputes. While deregulation is important, India needs a balanced approach that targets transaction costs while maintaining the rule of law.
venue: Zenodo (CERN European Organization for Nuclear Research)

title: NMA: Network meta-analysis based on multivariate meta-analysis and meta-regression models in R
abstract: Abstract Network meta-analysis has become an established methodology within systematic reviews for comparing the effectiveness of multiple treatments and is now a standard approach in comparative effectiveness research. However, the underlying statistical methods are often highly technical for non-statisticians in practice. To complement existing software, we developed NMA , a comprehensive R package organized around the multivariate meta-analysis and meta-regression framework and designed to provide a broad range of analytical and graphical tools through simple commands. The NMA package provides tools for evidence synthesis, network meta-regression, assessment of heterogeneity and inconsistency, comparative effectiveness analyses, and graphical visualization. It also incorporates higher-order inferential and prediction procedures and data-handling functions that facilitate the integration of arm-level data and summary effect estimates. In this article, we provide a gentle introduction to the NMA package and illustrate its application through a case study of a network meta-analysis of antihypertensive drugs.
venue: Research Synthesis Methods

title: Asymmetric Dependence Structure Between Climate Risk Volatility and Chinese Crude Oil Futures Commodity Price Using Copulas
abstract: Outlining the volatility of climate risk has become increasingly important in the financial sector. This study examines the correlation between climate change risk, economic policy, and Chinese crude oil futures. The dynamic copulas approach is used to assess both overall and tail dependence. A significant relationship exists between Chinese crude oil futures and climate uncertainty (CU) as well as climate policy uncertainty (CPU). Our study suggests that there are weak relationships with economic policy uncertainty that are clearly independent of climate conditions. The study highlights the significant pattern of right-tail dependence as opposed to left-tail dependence. It suggests that the pairs show minimal or no correlation when the index is low. The findings offer a new perspective on the links between Chinese crude oil futures, climate, and economic policy uncertainty. The empirical results show a strong time varying and asymmetric dependence between Chinese crude oil futures and climate related indices of uncertainty, particularly in the upper tail under high uncertainty conditions. On the contrary, there is a relatively low degree of dependence for economic policy uncertainty. These findings have significant implications for risk management, portfolio allocation and monitoring of climate-related financial risks in the emerging energy markets.
venue: Journal of Statistical Theory and Applications

title: Act2Intention: A Benchmark For Developing Active Mobile Agents Through Inferring User Intention from GUI Actions
abstract: Mobile GUI Agents powered by multimodal large language models (MLLMs) show promise in human-computer intelligence. However, current research primarily focuses on reactive task execution while lacking a comprehensive “understanding-prediction-execution” process for user intentions, which are the core requirements of active agents. In this paper, we propose the Act2Intention framework that builds an active mobile agent by integrating understanding, predicting user intentions, and executing decisions. Firstly, we constructed the Act2Intention Bench through collection and validated generation, comprising 72,511 intentions and over 700,000 actions across 52 apps, thereby establishing the first benchmark for evaluating proactive agents via continuous “intention-actions” trajectories. We further develop the Act2Intention Agent, achieving proactive services through Proactive-oriented Intention Understanding, Personalized Proactive Intention Prediction, and Experience-guided Intention Execution. Experimental results show that supervised fine-tuning on Act2Intention Bench yields absolute improvements of +32.0 Acc-S, +10.25 Acc-S, and +6.9 SSR points over non-fine-tuned counterparts under the same agent framework for intention understanding, prediction, and execution, respectively. This success underscores the necessity and value of the Act2Intention Bench, which establishes a standardized platform for developing and evaluating proactive agents and consequently paves the way for research on intention-driven human-computer interaction. To facilitate further research, we open-source our code and Act2Intention Bench at: npuNancy/Act2Intention.
venue: Proceedings of the ACM on Interactive Mobile Wearable and Ubiquitous Technologies

title: Quantifying the direct and indirect impact of COVID-19 vaccination: evidence from Victoria, Australia
abstract: Vaccines not only directly protect vaccinated individuals but also contribute to protecting the entire population via indirect herd-immunity benefits. However, researchers have long struggled to quantify these indirect effects at the population level, hindering the assessment of vaccination programme effectiveness. We developed a new method to estimate these effects, thereby markedly improving measures of the number of infections, hospitalizations and deaths averted by vaccination. Our population-based analysis of 6 440 000 residents of Victoria, Australia, reveals strong indirect effects during the Delta outbreak (September-November 2021). By modelling a non-vaccination counterfactual, we conservatively estimate 315 000 infections were averted (95% Bayesian credible interval (BCI): 231k-406k), as well as 33 400 hospitalizations (95% BCI: 22k-46k), and 4900 deaths (95% BCI: 2.8k-7.2k). These are 4.0, 7.5 and 8.0 times higher, respectively, than observed. Half of the averted infections and around one-quarter of hospitalizations and deaths were attributable to indirect protection. Homogeneous vaccination across local government areas could have reduced outcomes by approximately 25%.
venue: Journal of The Royal Society Interface

title: In preprints – making blood stem cells: how close is close enough?

title: Condorcet Cycles, Contextuality, and the Emergence of Quantum-like Collective States
abstract: The Condorcet paradox is traditionally viewed as a macro-level phenomenon of collective decision-making, showing that individually rational agents with coherent and transitive preferences may nevertheless generate socially intransitive majority outcomes. This interpretation assumes that cyclicity emerges exclusively through aggregation. In this study, we distinguish between micro-Condorcet dynamics, arising from contextual interactions within individual decision processes, and macro-Condorcet dynamics, emerging through majority aggregation. To investigate the relationship between these two levels, we introduce a minimal contextual model in which pairwise decisions are generated sequentially and linked through a contextual coupling mechanism. Although individual agents remain locally coherent and entirely classical at the microscopic level, each decision modifies the context of subsequent comparisons. Simulation results show that increasing contextuality progressively increases the probability of both micro- and macro-level Condorcet cycles. The transition between the two levels is strongly influenced by heterogeneity in decision thresholds, particularly those governing intermediate and closing comparisons. Rather than being driven primarily by initial preference relations, collective cycles emerge from heterogeneous evaluations of intermediate alternatives, which amplify contextual effects and facilitate cycle closure. A critical contextuality threshold is observed beyond which classical representability breaks down and no probability distribution over transitive preference rankings can reproduce the observed pairwise preference probabilities. These findings suggest that quantum-like probabilistic structures may emerge naturally as higher-level representations of contextual collective decision systems.
venue: Entropy

title: The economic burden of Borderline Personality Disorder: direct and indirect costs, and evidence from evaluations of interventions
abstract: Background Borderline Personality Disorder (BPD) is characterized by longstanding patterns of difficulty in functioning, and when left untreated, BPD can impose a substantial financial burden on individuals and society, in terms of higher healthcare costs as well as broader societal costs. Aims To conduct a critical review of the direct and indirect costs related to BPD. Additionally, to critically evaluate the economic evidence on interventions for BPD. Methods A comprehensive search strategy was conducted across PsycINFO, PubMed, and SCOPUS. Studies were screened in two phases: an initial title and abstract review, followed by full-text screening against a predefined eligibility criteria. Results Across 23 studies, high direct and indirect costs were consistently reported. Economic evaluations primarily examined established psychological interventions for BPD, such as Dialectical Behavior Therapy (DBT), Cognitive Behavior Therapy (CBT), and Schema-Focused Therapy (SFT), comparing costs and quality-of-life outcomes, with most demonstrating cost savings through reduced inpatient and emergency service use. Conclusions This review highlights the substantial economic burden of BPD, driven by high service use, productivity losses, and unmet needs. While interventions such as DBT, CBT and SFT show potential cost-effectiveness, inconsistent cost definitions and the omission of key components, including informal care and long-term impairment, likely lead to an underestimation of true costs. More comprehensive and standardized economic evaluations are needed.
venue: Frontiers in Psychiatry

title: Cultural Risk and Protective Factors Associated With Sexual Assault Among Hispanic and Non-Hispanic White Women
abstract: There is a paucity of research on sexual assault among Hispanic college women. Existing studies indicate that Hispanic college women, relative to non-Hispanic White women, report similar mental health sequelae following a sexual assault; thus, factors that protect or increase their risk are an area worthy of further investigation. Emerging research suggests that Latino cultural values, such as familism, social affiliation, and ethnic identity, may serve as protective factors for sexual assault among Hispanic college women, while acculturation with mainstream culture and perceived discrimination may function as risk factors. A substantial body of research also has found that alcohol and cannabis use increase risk for sexual assault. This study examined whether ethnicity moderated the effects of cultural protective and risk factors on sexual assault experiences among Hispanic and non-Hispanic White college women. Participants included 329 college women who completed self-report questionnaires on cultural factors, alcohol and cannabis use, and sexual assault history since the age of 14. Ethnicity was associated significantly with sexual assault severity, with Hispanic women, relative to non-Hispanic White women, reporting less severe sexual assault experiences. Perceived discrimination was associated positively with sexual assault severity among both Hispanic and non-Hispanic White women, as was greater alcohol and cannabis use. These findings highlight the importance of exploring additional cultural factors that may influence sexual assault risk among non-Hispanic White and Hispanic college women.
venue: Journal of Interpersonal Violence

title: General Theory of Structural Constraints: Investment Trap, Demand-Constrained Growth, and Regime Shifts in Monetary Policy Transmission
abstract: This paper presents a diagnostic theory that interprets a phenomenon observed in advanced economies—monetary easing and standard macroeconomic policies no longer generating sustained growth, even as they are accompanied by improvements in employment—not as a "failure of policy management" or a temporary demand shortfall, but as the structural depletion of investment outlets. As its core concepts, this paper introduces the structural frontier coefficient Φ, which represents the latent constraint determined by demographics, the institutional environment, and capital structure, and the critical threshold θ, at which policy effects undergo a qualitative shift. It further presents the "demand-constrained growth hypothesis" as the mechanism through which the structural frontier becomes constraining as the economy matures. The paper divides demand-side constraints into four types of goods—time-constrained goods, goods with strong ownership constraints, goods with weak ownership constraints and multiple ownership, and conduit goods—and organizes demand displacement and qualitative-improvement constraints as cross-cutting constraints superimposed on them. In an economy whose room for quantitative expansion has shrunk, the center of growth shifts to qualitative improvement; however, as the quality frontier is approached, the marginal cost of improvement rises while marginal utility and the scope for price pass-through may decline, so that technological progress may diverge from growth in sales and GDP. In the region Φ > θ, Solow-type growth theory and New Keynesian transmission may, by and large, function effectively, whereas in the region Φ ≤ θ, the spillover of monetary easing to real investment and sustained growth weakens, and easing tends instead to spill over into alternative channels such as asset prices, fund retention, and external capital movements. On the other hand, because the sensitivity of the employment channel to Φ is relatively lower than that of the growth channel, employment responses may remain relatively intact even in the region Φ ≤ θ. This asymmetry of the dual channels explains the simultaneous occurrence of employment improvement and growth stagnation. Under the definitional constraint that Φ is not back-calculated from outcome variables, this paper presents a two-layer diagnostic identification procedure. The structural state is diagnosed from the component-wise directions (structural signature) of the ordinal scale Φ̂, which is constructed without using outcome variables, and from the binding constraint; the policy transmission state is classified separately by the responses of the growth and alternative channels to identified monetary policy shocks (employment responses are checked as an auxiliary diagnosis); the two are then compared, with the estimate a of the realized investment ratio α, the cost-push coefficient κ, and other measures reported alongside as auxiliary findings. Furthermore, under the hypothesis that in mature, constrained regimes the elasticity of substitution declines and the dominant bottleneck determines the viability of investment, the paper positions the min approximation not as a predictive function but as a diagnostic limit. Companion empirical paper. This record also contains the companion empirical paper, "Does a Structural-Constraint Diagnosis Predict the Effectiveness of Monetary Easing? Exploratory Evidence from Within-Country Comparisons with Judgments Fixed before Matching" (Version 2, September 2026; English and Japanese PDFs, files named Watanabe_2026_*_Empirical_v2.pdf), which tests the central proposition of this paper.
