title: Order-Four Ordinal Patterns of Time-Changed Brownian Motion: Equal-Lag Detection of Reversible Volatility Clocks
abstract: The equal-lag order-3 ordinal statistics of a time-changed Brownian motion are exactly blind to every reversible independent volatility clock, so that clock detection there requires unequal lags (Adibi, 2026). We show that this blindness does not persist at order four. All twenty-four order-4 pattern probabilities of a time-changed Brownian motion with an independent clock admit an exact conditional representation as centred trivariate Gaussian orthant probabilities, a sum of three arcsines of the clock-increment correlations. Under a reversible independent clock the available symmetry is the Klein four-group generated by the global sign flip and time reversal. Its action partitions the patterns into eight orbits, equal within themselves but, unlike the order-3 turning patterns, not all pinned to their Brownian values. Two orbits, carrying exactly half the probability mass, remain blind to every stationary reversible clock; each of the other six moves under some such clock, subject to three exact linear relations, and all six move under the multifractal clock. For the lognormal multifractal random measure we prove a closed-form equal-lag deviation, \[p^MRW_ - p^BM_ \;=\; ^2\, _ \;+\; O( ^4), _4 \;:=\; _1342 \;=\; 2128 \, 16243,\] the coefficient of largest magnitude, with every orbit coefficient elementary in 2, 3 and surds. By exact stochastic scale invariance the deviation is independent of the sampling lag and of the integral scale at every intermittency. The common multifractal drift cancels, the exact opposite of the order-3 mechanism, and the deviation is pure curvature: the Hessian of the orthant probability contracted against the log-clock covariance. Order-4 ordinal patterns therefore detect a reversible multifractal clock at equal lags, a cleaner channel than the order-3 unequal-lag deviation. With optimal contrasts it is about five times cheaper to resolve, whatever the order-3 window ratio, though at plausible intermittencies it remains a high-frequency observable requiring of order 10^5 patterns. We give a model-free expansion with explicit third-order remainder, sharpened to the rate O( ^4), and an estimator-design analysis showing the orbit-count vector is sufficient. We prove the leading-order expansion and equal-lag detection at every pattern order n 4, identify two closed-form thresholds across pattern order, and evaluate the order-five coefficients from the Plackett reduction, which predict the orbits a direct simulation resolves.

title: Students will examine the relationship between sleep quality and cognitive performance.Students will explore the association between sleep quality and cognitive functioning.
abstract: Abstract Sleep is an essential physiological process, which is important for physical health, psychological and cognitive functioning. This review explores the link between sleep quality and cognitive functioning, focusing on memory, attention, working memory and executive functioning. The review is based on 15 relevant studies from the period 2015 to 2023. The literature that was selected covered studies with both subjective (self-report questionnaires) and objective (actigraphy and polysomnography) sleep assessment. The reviewed evidence revealed a relationship between poor sleep and deficits in cognition in a number of domains, with specific focus on sleep fragmentation and sleep deprivation. The results also show significant discrepancies between subjective and objective assessment of sleep quality. Placebo-like (and sometimes nocebo-like) effects of psychological factors such as belief and expectation about sleep on cognitive outcome may occur independently of physiological sleep parameters. Possible mechanisms of sleep–cognition relationship are changes in neural connectivity, neurochemical processes, synaptic plasticity, and sleep-dependent memory consolidation. Methodological differences, self-reported measures, and lack of long-term data in most cases however make it difficult to establish definite causal relations. In conclusion, the review shows that sleep quality is a significant factor in cognitive health and those physical and mental aspects of sleep need to be taken into account when assessing cognitive abilities. Longitudinal and experimental designs with standardized subjective and objective assessment should be implemented in future research to further elucidate these relationships and to create effective interventions.

title: Apothecary Readership and Print-Culture Reception of the Regimen-Sanitatis Workflow (1477–1501)
abstract: The Voynich Manuscript (Beinecke MS 408, c.1404–1438) is read here against a six-section court-physician workflow (astronomical / zodiac, herbal, the f58r preparation hinge, balneological, pharmaceutical, recipes) that the substrate registers as a structural rather than a decorative organisation [1]. The same workflow is independently legible in late-fifteenth-century early-print regimens addressed to a working apothecary readership. The 1477 Bologna incunabulum issued by Domenico de' Lapi for Sigismondo de' Libri (ISTC ib00314000), binding three regimen authors (Benedetto Reguardati of Norcia, Johannes Hispalensis, and Taddeo Alderotti) into one quarto, contains on folios 278–279 a printed two-column Latin quid-pro-quo substitution table citing Galenist authority (inquit Galienus) [2, 3]. Substitution tables of this kind belong to the operational shelf of an apothecary, not to the leisure shelf of a courtier or the abstract shelf of a scholastic. The same readership signature is cautiously visible in Wellcome MS.438 (Laufenberg + Salernitanus, later-fifteenth-century): the official catalogue records early ownership by Hans Jakob vom Staal and later acquisition in 1880 by the Basel apothecary Christian Gotthold Theodor Engelmann [4]. That later apothecary ownership supports an apothecary-readership comparison, but not historical use in a Langenthal working shop. Owner annotations attested on surviving copies of the Benedetto 1477 print indicate working apothecary use at presence-of-marginalia level; the specific transcriptions remain pending photographic re-validation [5]. At publisher/imprint level, the Bolt monographs describe approximately one thousand named apothecaries across some eighty-five towns from 1200 to 1600 [6, 9, 12]; the substrate's exact 1,029 / 85 / fourteenth-to-sixteenth-century formulation is internal and is not reproduced from the books here. The Bolt corpus is uncited in any Voynich publication located by the 2026-04-26 cross-reference-engine relay across the venues enumerated in [13]. The present paper does three things. Under the proposed six-section reading of MS 408, the 1477 print supplies a comparator for a regimen and apothecary workflow; this comparison does not establish identical content or historical readership of MS 408. It documents the editorial decisions of the 1477 print, most pointedly the embedded quid-pro-quo substitution table, as operational apothecary infrastructure. And it argues that the print-culture reception of the regimen-sanitatis genre, anchored on a Burgundian-state apothecary corpus that the Voynich field has not engaged, is the substrate-anchored entry into MS 408's pharmaceutical lane. The argument is not that MS 408 is itself a printed book; the argument is that MS 408 sits inside a workflow whose operational target audience is exactly the audience the 1477 print was edited for. title: Decision making of the selection tool of pattern recognition using trigonometric (ρ, ∝) spherical fuzzy set
abstract: A novel technique for creating complex tangent trigonometric (ρ, ∝) spherical fuzzy set is presented in this study. The concepts of complex tangent trigonometric (ρ, ∝) spherical fuzzy weighted averaging, weighted geometric, generalised weighted averaging and generalised weighted geometric will be discussed in this article. We calculated the geometric and weighted average using an aggregating model. The following algebraic methods will be used to further analyze several sets having significant properties. We also apply these operators to a variety of multiple attribute decision-making scenarios. The practical applications of ED, HD, and score values are demonstrated by a number of real-world scenarios. Furthermore, the complex tangent trigonometric (ρ, ∝) spherical fuzzy number has idempotency, boundedness, commutativity, and monotonicity. They are more familiar, reasonable, and competent to identify the best choice. Our goal was to evaluate the criteria with expert opinions to identify the optimal choice.

title: Price Setting before and during the Pandemic: Evidence from Swiss Consumer Prices
abstract: Abstract Using microdata underlying the Swiss consumer price index from 2008 to 2025, we document new features of price rigidity and assess their implications for inflation dynamics. The frequency of price changes increased in the decade before the pandemic, driven by items shifting to online price collection, as confirmed by causal identification from an event study around a collection‐mode switch. During the pandemic, the aggregate frequency response was muted, masking large cross‐sectional heterogeneity: demand contractions and stricter government interventions each reduced the frequency of adjustments, while demand contractions amplified their size. In response to aggregate shocks, firms adjust mainly the size rather than the frequency of price changes, consistent with time‐dependent pricing. However, nonlinear local projections reveal that when price flexibility is high or price selection is strong, firms respond along both margins, monetary nonneutrality falls, and the appropriate macro model switches from time‐dependent to state‐dependent.

title: The Twelve-Component Computational Apparatus of BSB Cgm 7958 (Hartlieb, Bavaria 1456) as Comparator-Lens for the Voynich Manuscript
abstract: We propose Bayerische Staatsbibliothek, München, Cgm 7958, a fifteenth-century Bavarian compilation in the Johannes Hartlieb stylistic tradition, date-locked to 1456 by a four-way computus colophon, as a primary-source-verified comparator-lens for the structural apparatus of Yale, Beinecke MS 408. Twelve apparatus components A–L are catalogued against the BSB digital facsimile, composed of nine folio-pinned components (C, D, E, G, H, I, J, K, L), each anchored to a specific folio surface with verbatim Bavarian Middle High German prose, and three umbrella categories (A, B, F) that name engine-level structures spanning multiple folios: a letter grid (A, umbrella), mod-9 / mod-19 / mod-28 / mod-30 arithmetic (B, umbrella, operations performed on other components), a weekday-value circle (C, fol. 16r), a nine-Capitel sum-lookup pair-result table (D, fols. 16v–18r), a four-quadrant outcome wheel (E, fol. 14r), an Aristoteles–Plato–Halij–Hartlieb on-page authority chain (F, umbrella, anchored at fol. 21v inside the broader Pythagoras–Ptolomeus–Plato–Aristotiles–Halij tradition cross-witnessed at Chart.A.558), a twenty-eight-mansiones-lunae table (G, fol. 2v), a planetary value-plus-colour table (H, fol. 20v), a twenty-five-row multi-exotic-alphabet inventory (I, fols. 22r–23v), a Latin sign-legend (J, fol. 23v), an iconographic legend (K, fol. 24r), and the dated sanctorale-plus-computus colophon (L, fols. 24v–25v). All nine folio-pinned components are verified against primary-source facsimile, with per-component completion gaps (component G 27/28 names, component J 8/10 entries, component K partial transcription) noted in the twelve-components section and listed as substrate-attested next moves in the implications and open frontier section. Five cross-witnesses (Gotha Chart.A.558, Heidelberg Cpg 3, Cpg 5, Cpg 65, Cpg 6) corroborate the apparatus at component level and place the tradition inside the MS 408 carbon-date window 1404–1438. The reading is comparator-lens, not identity claim: the known apparatus is the lens, the open manuscript is the target, and a substrate-anchored differentiator method scores residual asymmetries against shared baseline. The named readings in the falsification matrix fail one or more tests recorded in this paper; this bounded result does not claim exhaustive refutation of every historical proposal. The comparator-lens reading is advanced as the substrate-anchored frame the paper defends. An independent 2026 statistical study by Layfield and Davis finds sequence-sensitive and section-sensitive distributional structure under its LSA design. That text-channel result is adjacent to, not confirmation of, this paper's apparatus-channel reading. The paper situates MS 408 as one branch within the Wittelsbach-Burgundian / Salerno-Frederick II / Padua-Prague / Upper-Rhine corridor, not its centre.

title: STOCKOUTS AS SYSTEMIC INDICATORS: OMNICHANNEL CONSISTENCY AND INVENTORY MANAGEMENT IN PARAGUAYAN RETAIL
abstract: Paraguayan retail is undergoing a change that goes beyond the adoption of digital channels: it extends to how companies coordinate work, share information, and make decisions. Tensions emerge when the commercial promise exceeds what operations can deliver, and they intensify when processes, systems, and decisions remain fragmented. Among the symptoms of this misalignment, stockouts stand out because they affect operational performance and erode customer trust. The conventional interpretation treats them as inventory-control failures. This study proposes an organizational and systemic perspective. Its purpose is to examine how omnichannel consistency, inventory management, and stockouts are related in Paraguayan retail, with attention to the organizational conditions that facilitate or hinder consistent execution. The study adopts a qualitative, documentary-analytical approach, complemented by professional experience in the sector. The analysis suggests that stockouts function as systemic indicators arising from three conditions: fragmented processes, inconsistent information, and decisions based on divergent objectives. Thus, omnichannel consistency does not depend exclusively on technological investment and can be understood as an emergent property of organizational coherence. The study contributes a framework that reframes stockouts as structural signals.

title: Prevalence and Risk Factors for Financial Toxicity Among Sarcoma Patients During and Following Treatment Across the Lifespan
abstract: ABSTRACT Background Financial toxicity (FT) describes the impact of cancer and treatment‐related financial burden. We evaluated the prevalence and risk factors for FT among sarcoma patients. Methods A sarcoma cohort was constructed to assess health outcomes. FT was measured via “COmprehensive Score for financial Toxicity” (COST), where lower scores indicate greater FT. COST scores were evaluated in association with patient demographics, clinical data, and psychosocial/functional domains (PROMIS‐57) using multivariable linear regression. Subgroup analyses evaluated patients on‐ versus off‐therapy. Results Among 1125 participants (515 on/610 off therapy), median COST was 27.0 (IQR 18.0, 35.0), with absent, mild, moderate, and severe FT seen in 55.4%, 29.2%, 15.1%, and 0.4%, respectively. Lower FT was associated with increasing age (+1.28; 95% CI 0.86, 1.70), male sex (+1.93; 0.78, 3.08), and higher income (+0.87; 0.72, 1.01). Increased FT was associated with non‐White race (−1.79; −3.41, −0.13), larger households (−0.73; −1.25, −0.22), metastatic disease (−2.36; −3.80, −0.91), and active treatment (−1.61; −2.97, −0.24). Subgroup analyses demonstrated similar results regarding age, sex, income, and metastatic disease among on‐therapy and age, income, and household members among off‐therapy. Eight hundred and thirty‐two participants completed both the PROMIS‐57 and COST. FT was associated with anxiety (−0.77; −1.45, −0.08), depression (−2.11; −2.96, −1.26), pain interference (−1.36; −2.17, −0.55), and sleep disturbance (−0.68; −1.35, −0.004). Conclusion Almost half of participants experienced FT. Risk factors included non‐White race, active therapy, larger households, and metastatic disease. Anxiety, depression, pain interference, and sleep disturbance were associated with FT. Screening for FT is needed to develop targeted interventions.

title: Childhood Environmental Unpredictability and Bedtime Procrastination Among Undergraduate Medical Students in South India: A Cross-sectional Study
abstract: Objective: To examine the association between retrospectively reported childhood environmental unpredictability and bedtime procrastination among undergraduate medical students in South India.Methods: This single-center cross-sectional online survey included 200 undergraduate medical students. Bedtime procrastination was assessed using the nine-item Bedtime Procrastination Scale (BPS; range, 9–45), and childhood unpredictability using the 38-item Questionnaire of Unpredictability in Childhood (QUIC; range, 0–38). Because the BPS has no validated diagnostic cutoff, scores were analyzed continuously. The primary analysis used Spearman rank correlation with bootstrap confidence intervals (CI), and robust linear regression was used to quantify the association. An additional multivariable model adjusted for age, sex, academic year, residence, and socioeconomic category.Results: The mean age was 18.8 years (standard deviation [SD], 1.1), and 67.0% of participants were women. Mean BPS and QUIC scores were 27.93 (SD, 7.19) and 9.39 (SD, 5.53), respectively. Overall QUIC score was weakly associated with BPS score (Spearman rho=0.242; 95% bootstrap confidence interval, 0.111–0.366; p<0.001). After adjustment for age, sex, academic year, residence, and socioeconomic category, a five-point higher QUIC score was associated with a 1.48-point higher mean BPS score (95% CI, 0.52–2.43; p=0.003). Three parental domains showed small exploratory associations after false-discovery-rate adjustment.Conclusion: Childhood environmental unpredictability showed a small positive association with bedtime procrastination. The cross-sectional, retrospective findings are hypothesis-generating and do not establish causality.

title: The Voynich Manuscript as an Operational Page-Architecture: Structural Provenance in the Paduan Medical-Computational Tradition
abstract: We argue that Yale Beinecke MS 408 (the Voynich Manuscript) is best treated as an operational page-architecture, a working-reference manuscript whose page architecture, operator-class vocabulary, and section-boundary behavior are the defining structural features, situated in the Paduan medical corridor, on parchment whose radiocarbon range is 1404-1438. We use the medieval book-class label breviarium as a shorthand for one well-attested member of the broader operational-document family, not as a load-bearing genre identification; the structural class is the claim, the Latin label is auxiliary. The parchment dates 1404-1438; the production date and place are inferences from structural, comparator, and corridor evidence rather than from the carbon date itself. The reportatio literature documented by Jacqueline Hamesse supplies a supporting comparator for compressed medieval academic note-taking, but it is not treated here as proof that MS 408 is a literal lecture transcript. We make no decipherment, semantic plaintext, authorship resolution, or cipher-solution claim. The structural class proposed here is compatible with the cipher-overlay boundary maintained in the underlying research framework. Five convergent lines of evidence support the model: (1) module-level section correspondence between the Voynich Manuscript and Salernitan regimina, Arabic multi-book compendia, and the synthetic medical-philosophical framework of Pietro d'Abano's Conciliator (c.1310); (2) quantitative operator-frequency analysis across two Paduan and Venetian medical corpora totaling 6.9 million characters, reporting function-dependent operator vocabularies that parallel Voynich cross-section token behavior (numerical analysis carried in body text; visual-evidence plates regenerated to layout-mode controls in this revision; see the caveat in the glyph and notation evidence section); (3) the Hamesse reportatio framework as a peer-reviewed comparator for compressed notation and textual transmission, not as a quantified explanation of Voynich statistics; (4) the Padua institutional node, the University of Padua, San Francesco Grande Hospital (founded 1414-1416), and the Natio Germanica, as a corridor-consistent provenance context adjacent to the parchment window; and (5) documented and supported manuscript comparanda attesting related iatroastrological and operational notation practices across northern Italian and German-speaking practitioner networks. The closest single dated Padua-orbit comparator from the Pinali holdings is Squarcialupi ms. Fanzago 2.I.5.28 (Biblioteca Medica Vincenzo Pinali, Padova, c.1400), which provides an uncompressed comparator from the same broad period; the colophon's copiato da stub indicates this is a copy of an earlier exemplar, so the c.1400 dating localizes the copy and not necessarily the place of origin. The load-bearing claim is that MS 408 is a downstream specialized application of an inherited Italian operational page-architecture, with cipher overlay, rather than a Padua invention ex nihilo.

title: A Comparative Study on the Detection Efficacy of CUSUM and CPA in Multidimensional Tests
abstract: Cumulative summation (CUSUM) and change point analysis (CPA) procedures are the two most widely used methods for flagging aberrant item responses, yet their relative merits have been examined almost exclusively in unidimensional settings. This study evaluated five person-fit statistics (PFSs) that have demonstrated strong detection power in earlier research: the CUSUM-based ( C i T , C i L A R D ), and the CPA-based ( L max , W max , R max ), in multidimensional testing scenarios. In addition, the Wald statistic was derived to a new form for multidimensional tests, which is much different from the unidimensional version. Both a simulation experiment and a case study were conducted to assess the performance of these PFSs in detecting back random response (BRR). Results showed that inter-dimensional ability correlation influenced detection rates, and this effect diminished as test length increased. Across all conditions, the newly proposed W max statistic achieved higher average detection efficiency than its competitors and exhibited the greatest stability.

title: The Dual-Benefit Threshold: Why No Transfer Replaces a Collective
abstract: A member of a community health pool pays every year and never claims. By insurance logic, she should be the first to leave. She often stays, and dual benefit is what holds her: her own return is worth more as the collective’s output grows, a coupling measured by the cross-partial δ ≡ ∂2W/∂G∂M between collective output G and personal benefit M, zero when the benefit separates. The coupling changes who exits: under separability the non-claimant leaves first; where the collective channels are legible and clear the premium, she renews, so the lemons selection is switched off. Two results carry the paper. A pool retains a stable, positive membership if and only if δ exceeds a critical value δ*, at which the participation dynamics fold in a saddle-node bifurcation; where the collective channels are closed to the member, the non-claimants leave first, an unraveling like Akerlof’s. And where δ > 0, what the collective adds differs across members by δ·G·ΔM, so no single cash transfer fits all, and the best one is out by half that gap: the coupling cannot be bought out. The testable content is about staying, not joining. Indian panel data show illness does not predict who joins, and delivered benefit predicts who stays; a five-year Nepal renewal panel shows the claimant–non-claimant gap widening with tenure on the log-odds scale, the sign the coupling predicts. Version note. Version 103 (30 September 2026) of the canonical statement of the dual-benefit factor DB of the Trinity Law S = T × C × DB. Dual benefit is defined as the complementarity between a member's private return and the collective output of a voluntary collective organization, the cross-partial δ = ∂2W/∂G∂M of the money-metric benefit, with DB = δ/δ_max. This deposit supersedes the conjunctive formulation of dual benefit in the authors' earlier deposits (Zenodo 10.5281/zenodo.17582549 and 10.5281/zenodo.17726291). Files. (1) DBP_Canonical_v103.pdf and .docx — main text, nine sections and Appendix A. (2) DBP_Online_Supplement_v5.pdf — full proof of Theorem 1, the worked example (Table 2) and supporting characterizations. (3) dbp_audit_checks.R — replication script in base R (no packages; run with Rscript dbp_audit_checks.R) that recomputes the worked example of the supplement (Table 2), the wedge of Theorem 4, the fold constant of Theorem 3, the constant of Lemma A.4.1 and the two-scale renewal interaction of Section 8.2; each line prints the manuscript value beside the recomputed value. All theorems, proofs, definitions, and interpretations of results are the authors' own; the tool was used for prose drafting, consistency checking, and formatting, and the authors verified every substantive claim before inclusion. After using this tool, the authors reviewed and edited the content as needed and take full responsibility for the content of the published article.

title: The Impact of Adverse Childhood Experiences on Non-Suicidal Self-Injury Among Korean Adolescents: Moderating Effects of Social Support and Risk Profiling of Vulnerable Subgroups
abstract: Purpose: This study examined the prevalence of non-suicidal self-injury(NSSI) among Korean adolescents and investigated the independent and interactive associations of adverse childhood experiences(ACEs) and social support with NSSI. Methods: Data from a descriptive cross-sectional survey of Korean adolescents were analyzed. Group differences based on NSSI status were evaluated using χ2-test or independent t-test. Hierarchical multiple logistic regression analysis was performed to determine the independent effects of ACEs and social support on NSSI, and to test whether social support moderated the relationship between ACEs and NSSI. Results: Over one-third of the participants reported a past-year history of NSSI. Cumulative ACEs were independently associated with higher odds of NSSI, whereas higher social support was independently associated with lower odds of NSSI, confirming its robust protective role. However, the interaction between ACEs and social support was not statistically significant, indicating that social support exerts a generalized protective effect rather than selectively moderating the association between ACE exposure and NSSI.Conclusion: These findings underscore the need for systemic, early mental health screening within school and community settings that comprehensively assesses ACEs, depressive symptoms, and self-injury risk. Furthermore, prevention strategies should prioritize multi-source support networks involving peers, educators, and professional counselors, alongside evidence-based interventions tailored to enhance emotion regulation and resilience.

title: Structural Differentiation in the Voynich Manuscript Zodiac Section (f70v–f73v)
abstract: This successor carries one conclusion: the examined zodiac figures are not all decoratively identical. It does not establish constitution-archetype encoding. The earlier f70v1-to-f71r pigment comparison paired Pisces with Aries and is therefore not a matched LIGHT/DARK sign comparison; it is retained only as an exploratory cross-sign observation and contributes no independent evidence. The surviving-leaf record is infull, so this paper does not assign a specific absent sign. The M28 name/gloss is not used to identify a figure: the current packet contains competing internal translations and no adjudicated primary-text locus. The zodiac section of the Voynich Manuscript (f70v–f73v) is commonly described as calendrical or astrological imagery. This paper's internal audit records five kinds of differentiation in the inspected panels: paired LIGHT/DARK renderings for Aries and Taurus; container-holding figures recorded only in the inspected Aries LIGHT and Taurus LIGHT panels; 3–5 larger elevated figures in each of four examined wheels; an otedy row at f73v.23 carrying the lattice coordinate ; and a clothed central figure recorded on f73v. These observations reject only the paper's narrow decorative-identity null for the inspected set. They do not establish constitution-archetype encoding, intentional cross-section routing, or fullness across uninspected or unresolved panels. The internal 12-sub-folio sweep table records four otedy strings: one at f72v1, one at f73r, and two at f73v; no uniform-null bootstrap has been run. Unreceipted comparator scores and unverified codex-level tradition placements are excluded from the evidence base. Per-figure mansion assignment remains a proposed follow-up requiring a labeled tradition comparator and reproducible image loci.

title: Service Quality and Customer Satisfaction In Rural Banking: A Comparative Study Of Public And Private Sector Banks In Marathwada
abstract: Abstract Service quality has become a major basis on which customers distinguish competing banks, particularly when products and prices are broadly comparable. This study examines how rural customers in Marathwada, Maharashtra, perceive the quality of services delivered by public and private sector banks and how those perceptions relate to satisfaction. Primary data were collected from 100 customers, comprising 50 customers of public sector banks and 50 of private sector banks, using a structured five-point Likert questionnaire. The instrument covered the SERVQUAL dimensions of tangibility, reliability, responsiveness, assurance and empathy, while three items measured customer satisfaction. The analysis employed descriptive statistics, Cronbach’s alpha, Welch’s independent-samples t-test, Pearson correlation and multiple linear regression. The private-sector group obtained higher mean scores on each of the five service-quality dimensions. Mean overall service quality was 3.04 for public sector banks and 4.15 for private sector banks; corresponding satisfaction means were 3.45 and 4.29. The between-group differences were statistically significant (p < .001). Overall service quality and satisfaction also showed a strong positive correlation (r = .832, p < .001). The regression model explained 70.4% of the observed variance in satisfaction, with tangibility emerging as the only statistically significant unique predictor. The findings highlight the relevance of both the physical service environment and dependable, customer-focused service processes in rural banking.

title: The Effect of Covert Narcissism on Relationship Addiction in Early Adulthood: The Double Mediating Effects of Distress Tolerance and Emotion Dysregulation
abstract: Background: This study examined the pathway through which covert narcissism leads to relationship addiction through distress tolerance and emotion dysregulation in early adulthood.Methods: Data were collected from 394 Korean adults aged 18–39 years who were recruited using online convenience sampling. Participants completed measures of covert narcissism, distress tolerance, emotion dysregulation, and relationship addiction. The PROCESS macro was used for data analysis.Results: Both distress tolerance and emotion dysregulation partially mediated the relationship between covert narcissism and relationship addiction. Their double mediating effect was also significant, and the direct effect of covert narcissism on relationship addiction remained significant. This pattern remained when gender was included as a covariate.Conclusions: Individuals with high covert narcissism are sensitive to negative evaluations and easily hurt, thereby lowering their capacity to tolerate distress and intensifying difficulties in emotion regulation. Subsequently, they attempt to fulfil their unmet needs through others and become excessively absorbed in relationships. Therefore, interventions may be more effective when self-compassion-based approaches are used first to strengthen distress tolerance, followed by emotion regulation skills training, such as dialectical behavior therapy.

title: Pharmaceutical Preparation Vocabulary and Cross-Section Connectivity in Voynich Manuscript Folio 58r
abstract: Folio 58r of the Voynich Manuscript follows the first herbal run but is not the direct boundary to the balneological section: later herbal material and the astronomical section intervene before f75r. This folio has been variously interpreted as a pharmaceutical index, an astronomical chart, or a patient entry selector. We present a falsification-tested analysis of f58r's vocabulary class distribution and cross-section connectivity that is consistent with a pharmaceutical preparation bridge interpretation. The s-class (Honeycutt Ai Labs corridor-attested gloss s=syrupus [corridor-attested]) is one of three co-dominant line-opener classes alongside y- and d-; the lattice's high-signal cross-section anchor block for f58r lists otaly, otal, and okaiin anchors, with otal chip-annotated as routing to balneological f75v.50 and pharma f99v.27, and ary and ytar reported as multi-section cross-section operators in the line bodies. Of four prespecified falsification tests, the corridor-attestation test (T2) passes within-substrate; the class-distribution (T1), connectivity (T3), and comparator (T4) tests are reported as "consistent-with" the preparation bridge interpretation and do not constitute strict falsification of the competing patient-constitution-selector hypothesis at the token level. The internal f58r record's stored folio comparator is the Hartlieb Kräuterbuch 9 corpus at score 0.6. A separate direct structural comparison with the Cgm 7958 mansion-entry format found no repeating ordinal/name-list/entry-header parallel; neither observation is a top-match proof of function. f58r's vocabulary profile is consistent with a function specifying the pharmaceutical preparation method (syrup, decoction, soak, oil class) for plant-derived substances at the point of transition from botanical reference to balneological application. This is an internal preparation-bridge model situated within the court-physician reference-system context discussed in Honeycutt Ai Labs P-004 (DOI 10.5281/zenodo.20392093) and P-009 (DOI 10.5281/zenodo.20391967), not a sequence established by those papers.

title: CompSphere AI: An AI-Powered Compliance Intelligence Platform for Chartered Accountants
abstract: CompSphere AI: An AI-Powered Compliance Intelligence Platform for Chartered Accountants This research paper presents a structured literature review of artificial intelligence technologies for improving compliance, auditing, and financial document processing workflows performed by Chartered Accountants (CAs). The study reviews 27 research papers published between 2019 and 2026, covering document intelligence, Optical Character Recognition (OCR), layout-aware transformers, financial Large Language Models (LLMs), Retrieval-Augmented Generation (RAG), contradiction detection, Explainable AI (XAI), Robotic Process Automation (RPA), and agentic AI. The paper identifies key limitations in existing approaches, including unreliable financial reasoning, multilingual performance gaps, insufficient explainability, and the lack of integrated workflows that maintain an auditable chain of evidence. To address these challenges, the study proposes a four-layer reference architecture consisting of an Ingestion Layer, Reasoning Layer, Verification Layer, and Orchestration and Governance Layer. The proposed architecture emphasizes traceability, human oversight, model governance, and evidence-based compliance verification. The research also highlights opportunities for applying AI to Indian regulatory workflows, including Goods and Services Tax (GST), Tax Deducted at Source (TDS), Income Tax Returns (ITR), and Ministry of Corporate Affairs (MCA) filings. This work aims to provide a foundation for developing reliable, explainable, and auditable AI-assisted compliance intelligence systems for Chartered Accountants. Keywords: Artificial Intelligence, Chartered Accountants, Financial Compliance, Document Intelligence, Large Language Models, Retrieval-Augmented Generation, Explainable AI, Agentic AI, Regulatory Compliance, Financial Auditing.

title: Empirical Evaluation of Activity Coordination Among Field Response Agencies Using ICT Solutions
abstract: This study empirically evaluates ICT-based coordination among Japanese disaster response agencies during the acute life-saving phase. Although national guidelines mandate inter-agency cooperation, agencies (fire services, police, and Self-Defense Forces) operate as self-contained silos with few joint verification drills. To overcome this structural barrier, we conducted two empirical experiments in FY2025. The first, a joint rescue drill in Aichi Prefecture evaluating a three-tiered coordination structure (prefecture, municipality, and field command), verified system functions for facilitating smooth activity coordination among response agencies. The second, a regional joint drill in the Chubu block testing cross-system data integration, focused on the real-time acquisition and layer-overlay sharing of vehicle passage records on SIP4D-Xedge and SOBO-WEB to secure access routes to isolated areas. Post-drill surveys and observational analysis confirmed high coordination achievement, demonstrating that a common operational picture (COP) was positively evaluated by participants and suggested the potential to support situational visibility and operational area division. Moreover, key technical requirements were identified, including offline caching/synchronization against tunnel communication blackouts and standardized UI symbology across agencies. Ultimately, effective coordination requires standardized sharing rules, platform integration into routine operations, and robust COP generation visualizing unit capabilities and passage records to accelerate life-saving efforts.

title: Dynamic Determination of the Margin Ratio Based on a Market State Indicator
abstract: Individual investors engaged in margin trading must themselves decide at what level to maintain the margin ratio of their account. This paper formulates an investment rule that sets this target level each quarter as a linear function of a continuous market state indicator (constructed from the change in the U.S. 10-year Treasury yield and from the VIX), does not make additional purchases of the NASDAQ100-linked asset through margin trading, and adjusts the difference with a gold-linked asset; the rule is frozen and published before the start of operation. In a simulation using yen-denominated monthly data from July 1991 to July 2026, compared with a fixed margin ratio of 132.08% that matches the average position ratio over the full sample period, the annualized return from January 1997 onward was 16.15% versus 14.06%, the Sharpe ratio 0.770 versus 0.700, the Sortino ratio 1.187 versus 1.057, and the regression intercept α 1.919% per year (Newey–West t-statistic 2.55). No additional margin (margin call) occurred in either account, but the minimum drawdown to margin call was smaller under this rule (24.72% versus 28.99%). However, because the coefficients include values transferred from prior studies and data from the same period were used to design the rule, these results are not treated as evidence of effectiveness. This paper presents a plan, with the comparison benchmark, evaluation metrics, and decision criteria fixed in advance, to evaluate the rule in a virtual account over the 120 months following publication.

title: Acceptance-Based Approaches for Recovery in Individuals with Trauma Experience: An Integrative Review
abstract: Background: This study examined the characteristics and recovery outcomes of acceptance-based interventions for individuals with trauma experience in Korea, using the psychological flexibility model as an analytic framework.Methods: Five Korean databases were searched, yielding 2,156 records; from these, fifteen intervention studies were selected. Intervention content was rated for each of the six processes and summarized using the triflex categories of open, aware, and active.Results: The program composition differed according to lineage. Five of the eight acceptance and commitment therapy-based programs addressed all six processes as distinct sessions, while six of the seven mindfulness-based programs were organized around awareness and did not address cognitive defusion or self as context. Committed action was the process least often identified as a distinct session. Recovery was operationalized mainly as symptom reduction, and acceptance showed the most consistent change, although this was measured less often.Conclusions: When developing acceptance-based interventions, processes that follow awareness training and recovery indicators beyond symptoms reduction warrant greater attention.

title: Tested Cipher Outputs Under a Corpus-Induced Voynich Alphabet-Distribution Scorer
abstract: This successor narrows the result from class closure to test-set discrimination. Across the retained v3 and v4 trials, the unciphered manuscript surface scores above the tested catalog outputs under a scorer induced from that same manuscript corpus. Uniform-over-chip proxy outputs cannot reproduce the manuscript's non-uniform opener distribution. That is an alphabet-distribution mismatch, not proof against every constructed cipher: biased encodings, distribution-preserving transforms, alternative tokenization, post-processing, and methods outside the implemented catalog remain open. The modern per-primitive rows are relabeled seed variants of one SHA256-CTR proxy, not executions of AES, ChaCha20, Kyber, NTRU, McEliece, BIKE, HQC, SPHINCS+, or Dilithium. They support a common-proxy result only. Signature-scheme rows are structural simulations and are excluded from encryption claims. The Cardano-grille length argument is conditional on the paper's unsegmented multi-cell token grammar; an alternative emission grammar remains open. The Block B audit result is 12 of 13 folios at strength 1.0, with f99v.27 below the sampling floor; the earlier 8-of-13 statement is superseded. The corpus-induced scorer is partly self-fit, and independent medieval-corpus controls remain necessary.

title: Green Economy and Sustainable Economic Development in Thane District, An Empirical Analysis
abstract: Abstract This study examines the interrelationship between sustainable financial development and the green economy in the Thane district of Maharashtra State. Primary data was collected from 200 respondents. The level of sustainable financial development and the green economy were assessed using questions based on a five-point Likert scale. Statistical analysis of the collected data was performed using the Jamovi software application. Percentage (%) and frequency (f) analysis were used to examine respondent characteristics, while mean and standard deviation ware employed to describe the two key variables; sustainable financial development and the green economy. Cronbach’s Alpha was used to test the reliability of the questionnaire; the obtained Cronbach’s Alpha value ware 0.649 for the green economy scale and 0.637 for the sustainable financial development scale. Subsequently, the scores for both components were combined. Pearson correlation analysis was conducted between sustainable financial development and the green economy. The resulting coefficients indicated a statistically significant positive correlation between these two variables (r = 0.668, p < .001). Thus, the finding suggests that an increase in the level of green economy practices enhances the likelihood of positive outcome associated with sustainable financial development. The study concludes that the efficient use of resources, environmental conservation and protection and the promotion of environmentally friendly initiatives are crucial for the Thane district of Maharashtra state.
